newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish farmers hail grain price rises, trade wary.
newsitem.headline: Turkish farmers hail grain price rises, trade wary.

text.p: Turkish grain farmers hailed a government decision to raise base prices for state purchases from the 1997/98 grain crop by an average 85 percent over last year's prices.

But grain traders, who cast doubt on the government's ability to pay for its planned $750 million of grain purchases, said the increase may be aimed at securing votes in elections which could be held later this year or early next.
"We welcome the government's base prices for wheat and other grains," said the Union of Agricultural Chambers (TZOB), an influential group representing Turkish farmers.
"We are very pleased with the prices (which are) higher than world grain prices," it said in a statement.

Turkish Agriculture Minister Musa Demirci said on Thursday the government grain office TMO would pay 33,000 lira per kg ($235.7 per tonne) for hard red wheat purchases in June, up 83.3 percent from a year earlier.
Annual inflation runs around 77 percent in Turkey, where some 14 million farmers grow grains and 10 million of these grow wheat.
Initial base prices announced include durum wheat at 44,550 lira per kg, hard white wheat at 36,300 lira, feed barley at 24,750 lira, rye and oats at 24,750 lira, and corn at 29,700 lira.
The prices will rise 2,000 lira every month to offset inflation.
Demirci said the TMO planned to buy 3.7 million tonnes of grain this year, including 2.5 million tonnes of wheat, up from 1.5 million tonnes of grain last year.
But traders and wheat flour-makers questioned how the government could pay for the purchases.
"The prices are good for producers but not so for traders," said Hurriyet Dogan, a grain trader and a senior official from the Izmir Trade Bourse.

"The TMO should buy quickly, whether in cash or via delayed payments, to reach its purchase target," he told Reuters, but added "I don't think the TMO can afford fast buying because of its financial difficulties."
Demirci said the TMO and the treasury had "made all preparations to finance the purchases".
He said the TMO would need $750 million in finance and would use all domestic and external means to provide for this. He did not elaborate.
Some traders said the faltering coalition government of Islamists and conservatives was "investing for elections" by trying to keep the farm vote happy.
"This is nothing but investing for general elections," said Ali Guvenir, deputy general manager of the flour milling and grain trading company Ozkasikci.
"I don't know where the TMO will find the money," for its planned purchases, he told Reuters.

Finance Minister Abdullatif Sener, from the Islamist wing of the coalition, said on Friday early polls might be held this October, but Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller's True Path Party wants them in March, 1998.
Banking sources said the Turkish treasury might tap international markets for a two-year, $250 million syndication to help finance grain purchases.
A farm official said the TMO could also use a scheme to raise funds under which it exports about 1-1.5 million tonnes of wheat with immediate payments but forward shipments, possibly in September.
